newsitem.title: BOLIVIA: Ex-dictator wins Bolivia's 1st round vote.
newsitem.headline: Ex-dictator wins Bolivia's 1st round vote.

text.p: Hugo Banzer, a right-wing general who seized power in a 1971 coup, on Sunday won the popular vote in Bolivia's presidential election, according to unofficial results.
But Banzer, of the Nationalist Democratic Action (ADN) party, failed to win a majority and will face the runner-up in a runoff in Congress next August.
With nearly 90 percent of the ballots counted by a TV station, four contenders were neck and neck for second place.
"We acted in an authoritarian way, I admit," Banzer told a TV interviewer after voting ended, referring to the drive to stamp out Marxist guerrillas during his 1971-1978 regime.
But he said "there was no other way to do it" because Bolivia, one of the poorest nations in Latin America, was going through a period of turmoil at the time.
Banzer vowed that if Congress makes him president when it meets in early August, he will "respect the law and serve the Bolivian people." The handover is slated for Aug. 6.
The unofficial data showed Banzer the first-round winner with 22 percent of the vote and four contenders almost tied for the second slot, with between 16 and 18 percent.

They were: Juan Carlos Duran of the ruling Nationalist Revolutionary Movement (MNR), former President Jaime Paz Zamora of the Revolutionary Left Movement (MIR), millionaire businessman Ivo Kuljis of the populist Solidarity Civic Union (UCS) and Indian candidate Remedios Loza of the Motherland Awareness (CONDEPA) party.

After being ousted himself in a coup in 1978 (one of nearly 200 in Bolivia's history), Banzer decided to embrace democracy, formed the ADN party, and ran five times for president, once winning the popular vote but losing a congressional runoff.

The ruling party candidate, Juan Carlos Duran, 47, has an honest but also an uncharismatic image. However, although opinion polls were placing him in third place, partial data was showing him with a one-point lead over Paz Zamora.
Paz Zamora, a democratic president between 1989-1993, has problems of his own -- the White House last year cancelled his entry visa due to his alleged links with drug-trafficking.

Paz Zamora, 58, denies the charges, but outgoing President Gonzalo Sanchez de Lozada, a staunch U.S. ally, has insisted that if Paz Zamora were to become the new leader Bolivia would be shunned by the international community.
Kuljis is a 43-year-old agro-industry and media businessman of Croatian background and Loza, 49, is an Aymara indian who wants to substitute Bolivia's free-market path with state-oriented economics.

Aside from tarnishing Paz Zamora's image, drugs were hardly a campaign issue in this Andean nation, which along with Peru and Colombia produces virtually all the world's coca leaf and cocaine, most of which finds its way to the inner-city streets of the United States.

Coca is part of everyday life for millions of native Bolivians who honour the ancient tradition of chewing its leaves or drinking them in tea and who see the cocaine problem as just a "gringo" aberration.

All major-party candidates have espoused the 12-year-old free-market and privatisation drive which has consistently elicited praise of the international financial community but which appears to be testing the limits of Bolivians' patience.

Sensing the discontent with railways, telephones and services whose post-privatisation rates have shot up beyond the reach of many Bolivians, most of whom live under the poverty line, Banzer has promised to "humanize" the economy.

Below that line are pure-blooded Quechua and Aymara Indians who still dress like and speak the tongue of their ancestors, even after leaving their lands for a spot of city sidewalk where many spread their goods for sale, usually on a piece of multi-coloured cloth knitted on their looms.
Besides the president and vice president, whose term will now be expanded from four to five years, Bolivians also chose a new Congress, comprised of 27 senators and 130 deputies.
